```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4.2,
                      out.width = "100%")
has_survey <- requireNamespace("survey", quietly = TRUE)
has_mgcv <- requireNamespace("mgcv", quietly = TRUE)
has_cobalt <- requireNamespace("cobalt", quietly = TRUE)
```

```{r packages, message = FALSE}
library(ipw)
library(survival)
```

ipw estimates **inverse probability weights**: each person is weighted by the
inverse of the probability of the exposure they actually received, given
their confounders. In the weighted data, exposure no longer depends on the
measured confounders, and a simple model of outcome on exposure, a
**marginal structural model (MSM)**, estimates the causal effect (Robins,
Hernán & Brumback 2000; van der Wal & Geskus 2011).

An analysis has three steps:

1. **Estimate the weights** with `ipwpoint()` (exposure measured once) or
   `ipwtm()` (exposure that changes over time), or from your own
   probabilities with `ipwprobtm()`.
2. **Check the weights** with `summary()` and `ipwplot()`.
3. **Fit the MSM** with the weights, and get **standard errors**: with
   `ipwvcov()` for binary exposures with logistic models (point treatment
   or time-varying), otherwise with a bootstrap that re-estimates the
   weights when they are well behaved (section 5).

| Function | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `ipwpoint()` | Weights for an exposure measured once (point treatment) |
| `ipwtm()` | Weights for an exposure that changes over time, and censoring weights |
| `ipwprobtm()` | Time-varying weights from probabilities you estimated yourself **(new)** |
| `ipwvcov()` | Standard errors for the MSM that account for the estimated weights (binary exposures, logistic models) **(new)** |
| `ipwplot()` | Plot the distribution of the weights |
| `tstartfun()` | Interval start times for counting-process (Cox) data |

> **New in ipw 1.4.0.** Sections marked **New** describe
> features added after ipw 1.3.2: count, gamma and log-normal exposures,
> smooth terms with mgcv, ATT, ATC and overlap weights (also for
> categorical exposures), standard errors that account for the estimated
> weights (`ipwvcov()`), `type = "all"` for
> categorical and survival exposures in `ipwtm()`, and `ipwprobtm()`.
> Existing calls give the same results as before.
> The formulas, code and rationale behind each new feature are in the
> [methods article](https://tranhung93.github.io/ipw/articles/methods.html).

**ipw or WeightIt?** For point treatments,
[WeightIt](https://ngreifer.github.io/WeightIt/) offers many more weighting
methods (machine learning, entropy and energy balancing, CBPS, ...),
estimands, balance diagnostics through cobalt and outcome models with
M-estimation standard errors. [ipw](https://tranhung93.github.io/ipw/) is designed for exposures that change
over time in long data with each person's own visit times, Cox models for
the time to the first switch or to censoring, exposures that switch back
and forth or recur, count and skewed continuous exposures, and analyses
with few dependencies. See the README and the article
[ipw, WeightIt and PSweight side by side](https://tranhung93.github.io/ipw/articles/ipw-and-weightit.html)
for a side-by-side comparison.

# 1. Point treatment: a binary exposure

We simulate a confounder `l`, a binary exposure `a` that is more likely at
high `l`, and an outcome `y`. The true causal effect of `a` on `y` is 10.

```{r simdat}
set.seed(16)
n <- 1000
simdat <- data.frame(l = rnorm(n, 10, 5))
simdat$a <- rbinom(n, 1, plogis(simdat$l - 10))
simdat$y <- 10 * simdat$a + 0.5 * simdat$l + rnorm(n, -10, 5)
```

`ipwpoint()` fits the exposure model (here a logistic regression) and returns
the weights. With `numerator = ~ 1` the weights are **stabilized**: the
marginal probability of the exposure goes in the numerator, which keeps the
correction but makes the weights much less variable.

```{r ipwpoint}
w <- ipwpoint(exposure = a, family = "binomial", link = "logit",
              numerator = ~ 1, denominator = ~ l, data = simdat)
summary(w$ipw.weights)
ipwplot(weights = w$ipw.weights, logscale = FALSE, main = "Stabilized weights",
        xlim = c(0, 8))
```

Stabilized weights should have a mean close to 1. The exposure models are
returned as well, so they can be checked like any regression:

```{r models}
coef(w$den.mod)
```

The weighted regression of `y` on `a` estimates the causal effect; the
unweighted regression is confounded by `l`:

```{r msm}
c(unweighted = unname(coef(lm(y ~ a, data = simdat))["a"]),
  weighted   = unname(coef(lm(y ~ a, data = simdat, weights = w$ipw.weights))["a"]))
```

For inference, the weighted model is usually fitted with robust standard
errors, for example with the survey package as in the JSS paper; see
section 5 for `ipwvcov()`, which also accounts for the estimation of the
weights, and the bootstrap.

```{r svyglm, eval = has_survey}
msm <- survey::svyglm(y ~ a, design = survey::svydesign(~ 1, weights = ~ w$ipw.weights,
                                                        data = simdat))
cbind(estimate = coef(msm), confint(msm))["a", ]
```

**Unstabilized weights** use `numerator = NULL` (the default), and
**truncation** caps extreme weights at chosen percentiles:

```{r trunc}
w.unstab <- ipwpoint(exposure = a, family = "binomial", link = "logit",
                     denominator = ~ l, data = simdat)
w.trunc <- ipwpoint(exposure = a, family = "binomial", link = "logit",
                    numerator = ~ 1, denominator = ~ l, data = simdat, trunc = 0.01)
rbind(unstabilized = summary(w.unstab$ipw.weights),
      stabilized   = summary(w$ipw.weights),
      truncated    = summary(w.trunc$weights.trunc))
```

## New: ATT, ATC and overlap weights

The weights above target the **average treatment effect (ATE)**: the effect
if everyone versus no one were exposed. With `estimand = "ATT"` the weights
target the effect **in the exposed** (exposed get weight 1, unexposed
p/(1 - p)); with `estimand = "ATC"` the effect **in the unexposed** (the
controls: exposed (1 - p)/p, unexposed 1); with `estimand = "ATO"`,
**overlap weights**, the effect in the people whose exposure was most
uncertain (exposed 1 - p, unexposed p, all between 0 and 1). Here p is the
fitted probability of exposure.

```{r estimands}
fit.estimand <- function(estimand) {
  wt <- ipwpoint(exposure = a, family = "binomial", link = "logit",
                 denominator = ~ l, data = simdat, estimand = estimand)$ipw.weights
  c(effect = unname(coef(lm(y ~ a, data = simdat, weights = wt))["a"]),
    max.weight = max(wt))
}
sapply(c(ATE = "ATE", ATT = "ATT", ATC = "ATC", ATO = "ATO"), fit.estimand)
```

The effect was simulated as constant, so all four estimands are 10 in
truth, and the differences between the estimates are sampling noise. The
ATT weights show why: unexposed people with a high probability of exposure
get weights above 100, which makes that estimate unstable, and the ATC
weights do the same for exposed people with a low probability of exposure. Overlap weights
never exceed 1, which helps when some people are almost always or almost
never exposed. With an effect that differs between people, the three
estimands differ in truth as well.

# 2. Point treatment: other kinds of exposure

## Categorical and ordered exposures

For an exposure with more than two categories, `family = "multinomial"` fits
a multinomial logistic model and `family = "ordinal"` a proportional-odds
model (with `link = "logit"`, `"probit"`, `"cauchit"` or `"cloglog"`).

```{r categorical}
set.seed(4)
cat.dat <- data.frame(l = rnorm(800))
eta <- 0.9 * cat.dat$l
cat.dat$dose <- cut(eta + rlogis(800), c(-Inf, -0.5, 0.8, Inf),
                    labels = c("low", "medium", "high"), ordered_result = TRUE)
w.ord <- ipwpoint(exposure = dose, family = "ordinal", link = "logit",
                  numerator = ~ 1, denominator = ~ l, data = cat.dat)
w.mult <- ipwpoint(exposure = dose, family = "multinomial",
                   numerator = ~ 1, denominator = ~ l, data = cat.dat)
rbind(ordinal = summary(w.ord$ipw.weights), multinomial = summary(w.mult$ipw.weights))
```

### New: ATT and overlap weights for categorical exposures

For a categorical exposure, `estimand = "ATT"` targets the effect in the
people at one level, the **focal** level: each person gets
P(focal) / P(observed level), so people at the focal level keep weight 1 and
the others are reweighted to look like them. `estimand = "ATO"` gives
**generalized overlap weights** (Li & Li 2019): (1 / P(observed level)) /
sum over all levels k of 1 / P(k). Both need `numerator = NULL`. For two
levels they are the binomial ATT and ATO weights; for the effect in the
controls of a categorical exposure, use `"ATT"` with `focal` set to the
control level.

```{r categorical-estimands}
w.cat.att <- ipwpoint(exposure = dose, family = "multinomial", denominator = ~ l,
                  data = cat.dat, estimand = "ATT", focal = "high")
w.cat.ato <- ipwpoint(exposure = dose, family = "multinomial", denominator = ~ l,
                  data = cat.dat, estimand = "ATO")
rbind(ATT.high = tapply(w.cat.att$ipw.weights, cat.dat$dose, mean),
      ATO = tapply(w.cat.ato$ipw.weights, cat.dat$dose, mean))
```

## Continuous exposures

`healthdat` contains IQ, monthly income and a health score for 1000
simulated people; IQ confounds the effect of income on health. For a
continuous exposure the weights use densities instead of probabilities, so a
numerator model is required.

```{r gaussian}
data(healthdat)
w.gauss <- ipwpoint(exposure = income, family = "gaussian",
                    numerator = ~ 1, denominator = ~ iq, data = healthdat)
summary(w.gauss$ipw.weights)
coef(lm(health ~ income, data = healthdat, weights = w.gauss$ipw.weights))
```

### New: skewed continuous exposures (gamma and log-normal)

Many exposures are positive with a long right tail, such as a dose or a
duration: most values are small and a few are very large. A normal model is
symmetric and fits that tail poorly, and the tail is where weights become
large. `family = "gamma"` (log link) and `family = "lognormal"` (a normal
model for the log of the exposure) are meant for such exposures; both
require positive values. Below, the dose is log-normal given `l`, and the
true effect of one unit of `dose` on `y` is 1.

```{r skewed}
set.seed(8)
n.sk <- 2000
sk <- data.frame(l = rnorm(n.sk))
sk$dose <- exp(0.5 + 0.5 * sk$l + rnorm(n.sk, 0, 0.6))
sk$y <- sk$dose + 2 * sk$l + rnorm(n.sk)
c(mean = mean(sk$dose), median = median(sk$dose))   # right-skewed

# weighted correlation of the dose (or log dose) with the confounder l
wcor <- function(x, w) cov.wt(cbind(x, sk$l), wt = w, cor = TRUE)$cor[1, 2]

fit.dose <- function(family) {
  w <- ipwpoint(exposure = dose, family = family, numerator = ~ 1,
                denominator = ~ l, data = sk, trunc = 0.01)
  wt <- w$weights.trunc
  c(cor.dose.l = wcor(sk$dose, wt), cor.logdose.l = wcor(log(sk$dose), wt),
    effect = unname(coef(lm(y ~ dose, data = sk, weights = wt))["dose"]),
    max.weight.untruncated = max(w$ipw.weights))
}
round(cbind(
  unweighted = c(wcor(sk$dose, rep(1, n.sk)), wcor(log(sk$dose), rep(1, n.sk)),
                 unname(coef(lm(y ~ dose, data = sk))["dose"]), 1),
  sapply(c(gaussian = "gaussian", gamma = "gamma", lognormal = "lognormal"), fit.dose)), 3)
```

Good weights make the exposure unrelated to the confounders, so the table
shows the weighted correlation of the dose (and of the log dose) with `l`,
next to the effect estimate and the largest weight. The weights are
truncated at the 1st and 99th percentiles (`trunc = 0.01`), because a few
extreme weights would otherwise dominate a single estimate.

Without weights, the dose is strongly correlated with `l` (about 0.56) and
the estimate (about 1.53) is badly confounded. The log-normal model, which
matches how the dose was generated, removes most of that correlation (about
0.17), gives the estimate closest to 1 (about 1.17) and has by far the most
moderate weights: its largest untruncated weight is about 38, against about
1800 for the gaussian model. The gaussian model puts almost no probability on
the long right tail, so the few people with a high dose get huge weights; the
gamma model lies in between. None of the models removes the correlation
completely here, partly because truncation trades a little bias for
stability.

Choose the family by looking at the exposure: if it is right-skewed and
looks bell-shaped after taking logs, use `"lognormal"`; if its spread grows
with its mean, `"gamma"`. Do not use them for an exposure that is roughly
symmetric: income in `healthdat` (mean and median both about 2700) is
modelled well by `"gaussian"`, and a log-normal model there gives a few
people with very low income enormous weights.

### New: count exposures (Poisson and negative binomial)

For counts, such as a number of visits, `family = "poisson"` fits a Poisson
model and `family = "negbin"` a negative binomial model (via
`MASS::glm.nb`) that allows more spread than the Poisson. Here the true
effect of each extra visit on `y` is 0.5.

```{r counts}
set.seed(6)
cnt <- data.frame(l = rnorm(1000))
cnt$visits <- rnbinom(1000, size = 2, mu = exp(0.5 + 0.4 * cnt$l))
cnt$y <- 0.5 * cnt$visits + cnt$l + rnorm(1000)
c(mean = mean(cnt$visits), variance = var(cnt$visits))   # variance > mean
w.pois <- ipwpoint(exposure = visits, family = "poisson",
                   numerator = ~ 1, denominator = ~ l, data = cnt)
w.nb <- ipwpoint(exposure = visits, family = "negbin",
                 numerator = ~ 1, denominator = ~ l, data = cnt)
sapply(list(poisson = w.pois, negbin = w.nb), function(x)
  c(effect = unname(coef(lm(y ~ visits, data = cnt, weights = x$ipw.weights))["visits"]),
    max.weight = max(x$ipw.weights)))
```

The variance is clearly larger than the mean, so the negative binomial model
is the better choice for these data.

## New: smooth terms with mgcv

A regression assumes a straight-line effect of each confounder on the logit
of the exposure probability. When the true relation is curved, the weights
leave residual confounding. Writing `s(l)` in a formula fits the exposure
model as a generalized additive model with mgcv, which estimates the shape
of the curve from the data. Smooth terms work in `ipwpoint()` for the
binomial, gaussian and Poisson families and in `ipwtm()` for the binomial
family. The true effect below is 2.

```{r gam, eval = has_mgcv}
set.seed(10)
nl <- data.frame(l = runif(2000, -2, 2))
nl$a <- rbinom(2000, 1, plogis(2 * sin(1.5 * nl$l)))
nl$y <- 2 * nl$a + 3 * sin(1.5 * nl$l) + rnorm(2000)

w.lin <- ipwpoint(exposure = a, family = "binomial", link = "logit",
                  numerator = ~ 1, denominator = ~ l, data = nl)
w.gam <- ipwpoint(exposure = a, family = "binomial", link = "logit",
                  numerator = ~ 1, denominator = ~ s(l), data = nl)
c(unweighted   = unname(coef(lm(y ~ a, data = nl))["a"]),
  linear.model = unname(coef(lm(y ~ a, data = nl, weights = w.lin$ipw.weights))["a"]),
  smooth.model = unname(coef(lm(y ~ a, data = nl, weights = w.gam$ipw.weights))["a"]))
```

`plot(w.gam$den.mod)` shows the fitted curve. A covariate that is simply
named `s`, `te`, `ti` or `t2` is treated as an ordinary variable.

# 3. Exposure that changes over time

## HAART and mortality (`haartdat`)

`haartdat` contains simulated follow-up of 1200 HIV-infected patients from
seroconversion, one row per 100 days. Patients can start HAART (`haartind`
becomes 1 and stays 1). CD4 count is a time-varying confounder: low CD4
leads to starting HAART and to death, and HAART raises CD4. Ordinary
adjustment for CD4 would remove part of the effect of HAART; weighting does
not.

```{r haartdat}
data(haartdat)
head(haartdat[, c("patient", "tstart", "fuptime", "haartind", "event", "cd4.sqrt", "dropout")])
```

`ipwtm()` with `family = "survival"` fits Cox models for the time to
starting HAART. With `type = "first"`, each patient contributes until HAART
is started, because afterwards starting is no longer a choice. A second set
of weights corrects for **informative censoring**: dropout also depends on
CD4.

```{r ipwtm}
w.haart <- ipwtm(exposure = haartind, family = "survival",
                 numerator = ~ sex + age, denominator = ~ sex + age + cd4.sqrt,
                 id = patient, tstart = tstart, timevar = fuptime,
                 type = "first", data = haartdat)
w.cens <- ipwtm(exposure = dropout, family = "survival",
                numerator = ~ sex + age, denominator = ~ sex + age + cd4.sqrt,
                id = patient, tstart = tstart, timevar = fuptime,
                type = "cens", data = haartdat)
summary(w.haart$ipw.weights * w.cens$ipw.weights)
ipwplot(weights = w.haart$ipw.weights, timevar = haartdat$fuptime, binwidth = 100,
        main = "Stabilized weights for starting HAART")
```

The MSM is a weighted Cox model for death with the product of the two
weights:

```{r haart-msm}
msm.haart <- coxph(Surv(tstart, fuptime, event) ~ haartind + cluster(patient),
                   data = haartdat, weights = w.haart$ipw.weights * w.cens$ipw.weights)
summary(msm.haart)$conf.int
```

`tstartfun()` builds the interval start times needed for such data from
the end times:

```{r tstartfun}
toy <- data.frame(patient = c(1, 1, 1, 2, 2), time = c(14, 34, 41, 0, 11))
toy$tstart <- tstartfun(patient, time, toy)
toy
```

Other families work in `ipwtm()` as well: `"binomial"` (pooled logistic
regression), `"multinomial"`, `"ordinal"` and `"gaussian"` (GEE, with
`type = "all"`).

## New: categorical exposures that switch back and forth

With `type = "all"`, every interval contributes the probability of the
category observed in it, so an exposure can move between categories in
both directions. This now works for multinomial and ordinal exposures. The
models are pooled over time, so **past exposure belongs in the formulas**;
here the previous dose level `dose.lag`.

```{r type-all-ordinal}
set.seed(3)
n.id <- 300
long <- data.frame(id = rep(seq_len(n.id), each = 4), time = rep(1:4, times = n.id))
long$l <- rnorm(nrow(long))
long$dose <- NA
long$dose.lag <- NA
for (t in 1:4) {
  rows <- long$time == t
  prev <- if (t == 1) rep(1, n.id) else long$dose[long$time == t - 1]
  eta <- -1 + 0.8 * long$l[rows] + 0.7 * (prev - 1)
  u <- runif(n.id)
  long$dose.lag[rows] <- prev
  long$dose[rows] <- ifelse(u < plogis(eta - 1.5), 3, ifelse(u < plogis(eta), 2, 1))
}
long$dose <- factor(long$dose, levels = 1:3, labels = c("low", "medium", "high"),
                    ordered = TRUE)

w.dose <- ipwtm(exposure = dose, family = "ordinal", link = "logit",
                numerator = ~ dose.lag, denominator = ~ dose.lag + l,
                id = id, timevar = time, type = "all", data = long)
summary(w.dose$ipw.weights)
ipwplot(weights = w.dose$ipw.weights, timevar = long$time, binwidth = 1,
        main = "Cumulative stabilized weights by visit")
```

## New: recurrent exposure events in survival models

`family = "survival"` previously allowed only `type = "first"`. With
`type = "all"` (Graffeo, Latouche, Geskus & Chevret 2018), the exposure
indicator marks an exposure event at the end of an interval, such as a new
prescription, that may happen **more than once** per person. An
Andersen-Gill Cox model is fitted on all rows, and each row contributes the
probability of the observed status over its own interval. The intervals may
be irregular and differ between people.

```{r survival-all}
set.seed(21)
n.id <- 300
rec <- do.call(rbind, lapply(seq_len(n.id), function(i) {
  k <- sample(3:6, 1)
  cuts <- sort(runif(k))
  data.frame(id = i, tstart = c(0, cuts[-k]), fuptime = cuts)
}))
rec$x <- rep(rbinom(n.id, 1, 0.5), times = as.vector(table(rec$id)))  # fixed covariate
rec$xt <- rbinom(nrow(rec), 1, 0.4)                                    # time-varying
rec$expo <- rbinom(nrow(rec), 1, plogis(-1 + 0.5 * rec$x - rec$xt))   # exposure events

w.first <- ipwtm(exposure = expo, family = "survival", numerator = ~ x,
                 denominator = ~ x + xt, id = id, tstart = tstart, timevar = fuptime,
                 type = "first", data = rec)
w.all <- ipwtm(exposure = expo, family = "survival", numerator = ~ x,
               denominator = ~ x + xt, id = id, tstart = tstart, timevar = fuptime,
               type = "all", data = rec)
c(rows.used.first = sum(w.first$selvar), rows.used.all = sum(w.all$selvar))
rbind(first = summary(w.first$ipw.weights), all = summary(w.all$ipw.weights))
```

With `type = "first"`, the rows after a person's first exposure event are
ignored; with `type = "all"` they all count. For a treatment that is
started and stopped, Graffeo et al. compute weights separately for starting
(on the rows off treatment) and for stopping (on the rows on treatment).

# 4. New: weights from your own probabilities

If you estimated the exposure probabilities yourself, for example with a
machine-learning model or SuperLearner, the weights are easy to form. For a
point treatment no function is needed: the stabilized weight is the
numerator probability divided by the probability of the exposure each
person actually received. Below, a cubic logistic model stands in for a
flexible learner.

```{r own-point}
p.flex <- fitted(glm(a ~ poly(l, 3), family = binomial, data = simdat))
den.own <- ifelse(simdat$a == 1, p.flex, 1 - p.flex)
num.own <- ifelse(simdat$a == 1, mean(simdat$a), 1 - mean(simdat$a))
w.own <- num.own / den.own
summary(w.own)
coef(lm(y ~ a, data = simdat, weights = w.own))["a"]
```

For time-varying data, `ipwprobtm()` does the part that is easy to get
wrong: it multiplies the ratios within each person in time order (the data
need not be sorted), returns the weights in the order of the input and can
truncate them.

```{r ipwprobtm}
toy <- data.frame(id = c(1, 1, 2, 2), time = c(1, 2, 1, 2), p = c(0.5, 0.8, 0.4, 0.9))
ipwprobtm(den = toy$p, id = toy$id, timevar = toy$time)$ipw.weights
```

For weights of `type = "first"` or `"cens"`, set the probabilities to 1 for
the rows after the first switch. The warning from `glm()` above is a
reminder of the main risk: flexible models can produce probabilities close
to 0 or 1 and therefore extreme weights. Check the weights and consider
`trunc`.

# 5. Standard errors: M-estimation, robust and bootstrap

## New: `ipwvcov()` for a binary point treatment and for time-varying weights

**What a variance-covariance matrix is.** The variance-covariance matrix
(vcov) `V` of a model describes the uncertainty of its coefficients. Its
diagonal holds the variances of the coefficients, and `sqrt(diag(V))` gives
their standard errors. The off-diagonal entries are covariances. You need
them for combinations of coefficients, such as `a + a:sex`, the effect of
`a` when `sex = 1` in a model with an interaction. Standard errors,
confidence intervals and p-values all come from this matrix. `vcov(fit)` is
R's standard function for it, and tools such as
`lmtest::coeftest(fit, vcov. = V)`, `lmtest::coefci()` and the
marginaleffects package accept a vcov that you supply. `ipwvcov()` returns
the vcov of the MSM coefficients, corrected for the estimation of the
weights.

**When you need it.** Use it when you want standard errors and confidence
intervals for an MSM that account for the weights being estimated. There
are two alternatives. Robust standard errors treat the weights as known:
for the ATE they are usually too large, and for the ATT, ATC and ATO they
can be off in either direction. The bootstrap with the weights re-estimated
in each sample is correct but slow. `ipwvcov()` does not cover Cox exposure
models (`family = "survival"`), links other than logit, truncated weights,
smooth terms (mgcv), exposures that are not binary (categorical, ordinal,
continuous, counts), or Cox MSMs with `strata()`. For these, use the
bootstrap (next subsection). With heavy-tailed weights, where a few people
carry much of the weight, neither `ipwvcov()` nor the bootstrap can be
trusted. Check `ipwplot()` and the effective sample size (section 6) first
(see "Heavy-tailed weights" in the
[methods article](https://tranhung93.github.io/ipw/articles/methods.html)).

`ipwvcov()` handles a binary point treatment with an MSM fitted with
`lm()`, `glm()` or `coxph()`, and time-varying weights (below). The
MSM and the exposure model(s) are solved together as one set of estimating
equations (M-estimation, Lunceford & Davidian 2004), and the sandwich
variance of all parameters is computed. It works for every estimand (ATE,
ATT, ATC, ATO), stabilized or not, and is the recommended option in this
setting. It is new and still experimental. Fit the MSM on the same rows as
`ipwpoint()`, with `weights = w$ipw.weights`:

```{r ipwvcov}
msm.lm <- lm(y ~ a, data = simdat, weights = w$ipw.weights)
se.mest <- sqrt(diag(ipwvcov(w, msm.lm)))
se.mest
```

For this model, `lmtest::coeftest(msm.lm, vcov. = ipwvcov(w, msm.lm))` gives
the Wald tests.

For a survival outcome, the MSM can be a weighted Cox model with one row per
person and `Surv(time, status)`. Below, a time to event is simulated for
`simdat` with a conditional hazard ratio of exp(-0.5) for `a` given `l`.
The MSM estimates the marginal hazard ratio, which for a Cox model is closer
to 1 even without confounding (hazard ratios are not collapsible), so the
estimate is not expected to equal -0.5. The robust standard error
of `coxph()` treats the weights as known; `ipwvcov()` accounts for their
estimation:

```{r ipwvcov-cox}
set.seed(5)
simdat$time <- rexp(nrow(simdat), 0.1 * exp(-0.5 * simdat$a + 0.05 * simdat$l))
simdat$status <- as.numeric(simdat$time < 10)
simdat$time <- pmin(simdat$time, 10)
msm.cox <- coxph(Surv(time, status) ~ a, data = simdat, weights = w$ipw.weights)
c(log.hr = unname(coef(msm.cox)),
  robust.se = sqrt(msm.cox$var[1, 1]),
  ipwvcov.se = sqrt(ipwvcov(w, msm.cox)[1, 1]))
```

```{r ipwvcov-cox-numbers, include = FALSE}
cox.est <- unname(coef(msm.cox))
cox.se <- c(robust = sqrt(msm.cox$var[1, 1]), ipwvcov = sqrt(ipwvcov(w, msm.cox)[1, 1]))
cox.ci <- lapply(cox.se, function(se) cox.est + c(-1, 1) * 1.96 * se)
fmt <- function(x, d) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = d)
show.ci <- function(ci) paste0("(", fmt(ci[1], 2), ", ", fmt(ci[2], 2), ")")
excludes.0 <- vapply(cox.ci, function(ci) ci[1] > 0 || ci[2] < 0, logical(1))
pct.smaller <- 100 * (1 - cox.se[["ipwvcov"]] / cox.se[["robust"]])
zero.text <- if (all(excludes.0)) {
  "Both exclude 0, so the gain is precision, not a different conclusion"
} else if (!any(excludes.0)) {
  "Both include 0, so the gain is precision, not a different conclusion"
} else if (excludes.0[["ipwvcov"]]) {
  "Here the `ipwvcov()` interval excludes 0 and the robust one does not"
} else {
  "Here the robust interval excludes 0 and the `ipwvcov()` one does not"
}
```

The `ipwvcov()` standard error (`r fmt(cox.se[["ipwvcov"]], 3)`) is
`r fmt(abs(pct.smaller), 0)`% `r if (pct.smaller >= 0) "smaller" else "larger"`
than the robust one (`r fmt(cox.se[["robust"]], 3)`). For the ATE, theory
predicts a smaller standard error: estimating the weights from the data
reduces the variance of the effect estimate, and the robust standard error
ignores that gain. The 95% confidence intervals for the log hazard ratio
(estimate ± 1.96 × SE) are `r show.ci(cox.ci$robust)` with the robust standard
error and `r show.ci(cox.ci$ipwvcov)` with `ipwvcov()`. `r zero.text`. In
other data, a difference of this size could decide whether an interval
crosses 0. Neither interval is expected to contain -0.5, because the MSM
targets the marginal hazard ratio, not the conditional exp(-0.5).

One data set cannot show which standard error is right. That needs a
simulation in which the true effect is known and the study is repeated on
many data sets. In the Cox simulation of the article
[ipw, WeightIt and PSweight side by side](https://tranhung93.github.io/ipw/articles/ipw-and-weightit.html#a-cox-outcome-model)
(1000 data sets of 500 people), the variance from `ipwvcov()` matched the
true variance of the estimates on average (ratio 1.00 for both estimands
studied) and its 95% intervals covered the truth in about 95% of the data
sets. The robust variance was 1.12 to 1.20 times the true variance (the
standard error 6 to 10% too large). The
[methods article](https://tranhung93.github.io/ipw/articles/methods.html#how-the-simulations-judge-a-standard-error)
explains how a simulation judges a standard error.

With tied event times, fit the Cox model with `ties = "breslow"`.

`ipwvcov()` also accepts **time-varying weights** from `ipwtm()` with
`family = "binomial"` and `link = "logit"` (pooled logistic models, any
`type`), alone or as a list whose weights multiply, such as treatment times
censoring weights. The MSM is fitted on all rows of the long data, with
`lm()`, `glm()` or a Cox model on counting-process data; the scores are
summed within each person. Below, the HAART analysis of section 3 with
pooled logistic models instead of Cox models for starting HAART and for
dropout:

```{r ipwvcov-tm}
w.start.bin <- ipwtm(exposure = haartind, family = "binomial", link = "logit",
                     numerator = ~ sex + age, denominator = ~ sex + age + cd4.sqrt,
                     id = patient, timevar = fuptime, type = "first", data = haartdat)
w.drop.bin <- ipwtm(exposure = dropout, family = "binomial", link = "logit",
                    numerator = ~ sex + age, denominator = ~ sex + age + cd4.sqrt,
                    id = patient, timevar = fuptime, type = "cens", data = haartdat)
msm.bin <- coxph(Surv(tstart, fuptime, event) ~ haartind + cluster(patient),
                 data = haartdat, ties = "breslow",
                 weights = w.start.bin$ipw.weights * w.drop.bin$ipw.weights)
c(log.hr = unname(coef(msm.bin)),
  robust.cluster.se = sqrt(msm.bin$var[1, 1]),
  ipwvcov.se = sqrt(ipwvcov(list(w.start.bin, w.drop.bin), msm.bin)[1, 1]))
```

The robust standard error with `cluster(patient)` treats the weights as
known; here the two are close. For the cases `ipwvcov()` does not cover
(listed at the start of this subsection), such as the Cox exposure models
of section 3, use the bootstrap below.

## Robust and bootstrap standard errors

Robust (sandwich) standard errors treat the weights as known. In
simulations of weighted Cox models, Austin (2016) found naive standard
errors too small and robust standard errors too large; the bootstrap that
**re-estimates the weights in each bootstrap sample** gave correct standard
errors and confidence intervals. Robust standard errors are not always
too large, though: they can be too small for a continuous exposure and for
time-varying weights (see below), and the bootstrap is then preferred.

A bootstrap takes a few lines: draw a sample with replacement, re-estimate
the weights and the MSM on it, and repeat.

```{r boot-point}
msm.effect <- function(d) {
  wt <- ipwpoint(exposure = a, family = "binomial", link = "logit",
                 numerator = ~ 1, denominator = ~ l, data = d)$ipw.weights
  coef(lm(y ~ a, data = d, weights = wt))["a"]
}
set.seed(1)
boot.est <- replicate(200, msm.effect(simdat[sample(nrow(simdat), replace = TRUE), ]))
c(estimate = unname(msm.effect(simdat)), bootstrap.se = sd(boot.est),
  m.estimation.se = unname(se.mest["a"]))
quantile(boot.est, c(0.025, 0.975))   # percentile 95% confidence interval
```

For data with several rows per person, resample **people**, not rows: keep
all rows of a sampled person and give each sampled copy a new identifier, so
that someone drawn twice counts as two people. Here both sets of weights for
the HAART example of section 3, which use Cox exposure models and so are not
covered by `ipwvcov()`, are re-estimated in each sample (use about 200
samples in practice; 20 keep this vignette quick):

```{r boot-haart}
haart.effect <- function(d) {
  w1 <- ipwtm(exposure = haartind, family = "survival", numerator = ~ sex + age,
              denominator = ~ sex + age + cd4.sqrt, id = patient,
              tstart = tstart, timevar = fuptime, type = "first", data = d)
  w2 <- ipwtm(exposure = dropout, family = "survival", numerator = ~ sex + age,
              denominator = ~ sex + age + cd4.sqrt, id = patient,
              tstart = tstart, timevar = fuptime, type = "cens", data = d)
  coef(coxph(Surv(tstart, fuptime, event) ~ haartind, data = d,
             weights = w1$ipw.weights * w2$ipw.weights))
}
rows.by.patient <- split(seq_len(nrow(haartdat)), haartdat$patient)
cluster.sample <- function() {
  pick <- sample(length(rows.by.patient), replace = TRUE)
  rows <- rows.by.patient[pick]
  d <- haartdat[unlist(rows), ]
  d$patient <- rep(seq_along(pick), lengths(rows))   # new id per sampled copy
  d
}
set.seed(2)
boot.haart <- replicate(20, haart.effect(cluster.sample()))
c(robust.se = unname(sqrt(diag(vcov(msm.haart)))), bootstrap.se = sd(boot.haart))
```

**When does the bootstrap help?** The
[simulation study](https://tranhung93.github.io/ipw/articles/simulations.html)
gives a mixed answer:

* For a point treatment with **good overlap**, the bootstrap standard error
  was accurate, while the variance from robust standard errors was 1.25
  times the true variance (the standard error 12% too large).
* For a **weighted Cox model** with good overlap, naive, robust and bootstrap
  standard errors were all close to correct.
* When some **weights are extreme**, through poor overlap (the `simdat`
  example above) or through products of time-varying weights over several
  visits, all standard errors were too small, the bootstrap ones included,
  and 95% confidence intervals covered the truth in only 57 to 80% of
  samples.

So the bootstrap does not repair unstable weights. Check the weights first
(section 6), and if some are extreme, consider truncation (`trunc`), overlap
weights (`estimand = "ATO"`) or a better exposure model before relying on
any standard error.

# 6. Checking the weights

* **Mean close to 1.** Stabilized weights should average about 1; a mean far
  from 1 suggests a misspecified exposure model.
* **Extreme weights.** Very large weights point to **positivity** problems:
  some kinds of people (almost) never receive one of the exposures. Look at
  `ipwplot()`, reconsider the model, use overlap weights (`estimand = "ATO"`)
  or truncate (`trunc`), keeping in mind that truncation slightly changes
  what is estimated.
* **Assumptions.** The weighted analysis assumes no unmeasured confounding,
  positivity, consistency and correctly specified exposure (and censoring)
  models.

## Covariate balance

Good weights make the confounders unrelated to the exposure, so after
weighting their distribution should be the same in the exposure groups.
Check this directly: it tests the exposure model where it matters. The
cobalt package (Greifer) computes balance statistics for any weights; ipw's
weights are passed as a plain vector, with `method = "weighting"`. The
standardized mean difference (SMD) uses the pooled standard deviation of the
unweighted groups (`s.d.denom = "pooled"`); absolute SMDs below 0.1 are a
common rule of thumb.

```{r balance-point, eval = has_cobalt}
cobalt::bal.tab(a ~ l, data = simdat, weights = w$ipw.weights,
                method = "weighting", s.d.denom = "pooled", un = TRUE)
```

Several sets of weights can be compared at once; `love.plot()` draws the
SMDs before and after weighting. Here the stabilized ATE weights and the
overlap weights from section 1:

```{r ato-weights}
w.ato <- ipwpoint(exposure = a, family = "binomial", link = "logit",
                  denominator = ~ l, data = simdat, estimand = "ATO")
```

```{r love-plot, eval = has_cobalt, fig.height = 2.6}
bal <- cobalt::bal.tab(a ~ l, data = simdat, method = "weighting",
                       weights = data.frame(ATE = w$ipw.weights, ATO = w.ato$ipw.weights),
                       s.d.denom = "pooled", un = TRUE)
cobalt::love.plot(bal, thresholds = c(m = 0.1), abs = TRUE)
```

With a logistic denominator model, overlap weights balance the mean of every
covariate in the model exactly (SMD 0). The stabilized ATE weights reduce the
SMD of `l` from about 2.2 to about 0.6, which is still far above 0.1: with
the poor overlap in these data, a few unexposed people with a high `l` carry
most of the weight (see the effective sample sizes below), and their
weighted mean of `l` is unstable. This is the same problem that made the ATT
weights extreme in section 1.

For time-varying weights, check balance at each time point among the people
for whom the exposure decision is made there. With `type = "first"`, these
are the rows with `selvar == 1` (not yet on HAART at the start of the
interval), and the groups are those who start HAART in that interval and
those who do not; the weight of each row is the cumulative weight up to and
including that interval. The censoring weights do not depend on whether
HAART is started, so only the HAART weights are used here.

```{r balance-haart, eval = has_cobalt}
at.risk <- w.haart$selvar == 1 & haartdat$fuptime %in% c(100, 500)
haart.sub <- haartdat[at.risk, ]
cobalt::bal.tab(haartind ~ cd4.sqrt + sex + age, data = haart.sub,
                weights = w.haart$ipw.weights[at.risk], method = "weighting",
                s.d.denom = "pooled", un = TRUE, cluster = "fuptime")
```

We show this example as it is, rather than picking a time point where the
weights look good, because a balance check is only useful if it can fail.
The result is mixed, and that is useful to know. At 500 days, weighting
halves the imbalance in CD4 count (SMD from about -0.8 to -0.4) but does not
remove it; at 100 days, where the few people starting HAART happened to have
a higher CD4 count, it over-corrects (SMD from 0.25 to above 0.9). The
denominator model is one Cox model with a single CD4 coefficient for the
whole follow-up; pooled over all at-risk rows, weighting reduces the SMD of
CD4 from about -0.47 to 0.13. Balance at single time points with only 30 to
50 people starting HAART is noisy, but a pattern like this suggests checking
whether the effect of CD4 on starting HAART changes over follow-up, for
example by adding an interaction with a time-period indicator to the
denominator model.

Sex and age are in the numerator as well as the denominator model, so the
stabilized weights deliberately leave them unbalanced: they must be adjusted
for in the MSM (e.g. `coxph(... ~ haartind + sex + age)`). Unstabilized
weights (`numerator = NULL`) would balance them too, at the price of more
variable weights.

## Effective sample size

Variable weights reduce the information in the data. Kish's **effective
sample size**, (sum of weights)^2 / (sum of squared weights), is the size of
an unweighted sample with about the same precision. Compute it overall and
by exposure group; a large drop in one group means a few people carry most
of the weight there.

```{r ess}
ess <- function(w) sum(w)^2 / sum(w^2)
rbind(n = c(all = nrow(simdat), table(simdat$a)),
      ATE = c(ess(w$ipw.weights), tapply(w$ipw.weights, simdat$a, ess)),
      ATO = c(ess(w.ato$ipw.weights), tapply(w.ato$ipw.weights, simdat$a, ess)))
```

`cobalt::bal.tab()` reports the same quantity by group under "Effective
sample sizes".
